newsitem.title: GREECE: SALONIKA ANGRY WITH SCORNFUL "ATHENS" POLITICIANS.
newsitem.headline: SALONIKA ANGRY WITH SCORNFUL "ATHENS" POLITICIANS.

text.p: Salonika, Greece's second biggest city, feels scorned by Athens' politicians and Prime Minister Costas Simitis will be the first one to feel the heat in his first major campaign appearance on Friday.

"We are sick and tired of words. We are sick and tired of the scornful central Athens authority. We welcome the political leaders but we won't accept any more rolling promises. We want deeds now," Salonika's conservative mayor Costas Kosmopoulos told Reuters.
Simitis will open an international trade fair in this northern port of a million residents on Friday and over the weekend he will outline his economic and foreign policy plans for next year.

"I wrote a letter to Mr Simitis and to all opposition leaders who will follow him here that we don't need their sympathy. Salonika needs major infrastructure works which have been forgotten in their drawers for years," Kosmopoulos said.
"I told them all that the trade fair is not a pre-election parade," he added.
The city's indifference to what is decribed as the "sinful capital" is particularly apparent in this campaign period.

Streets have no pre-election banners and residents choose to spend the summer's remainder in nearby beaches, tavernas and bars rather than watching heated political debates on television or participating in party activity.

"I would not be surprised if many cast blank votes in the countryside, including Salonika, to express their protest," an official in Simitis's PASOK party said. "The countryside feels abandoned and it blames all recent governments."

Salonika was always considered the barometer of the Greek political scene as huge pre-election rallies of hundreds of thousands of voters at the start of each campaign gave a good indication on who the winner would be.
But Simitis' socialist party and most opposition parties have called for no rallies outside Athens in this election campaign and Salonika doesn't seem to mind.

"In the past 20 years my taxi has been a political battlefield," Renos Pitaras, a cab driver, said. "My customers argued non stop during campaign periods but now they don't seem to care. Athens is another place and the politicians are in Athens."

Kosmopoulos charged that works like a city metro, underground garages, improvements at the airport and other projects have been pending for years. A major Balkan trading centre, Salonika, has been named Europe's cultural capital for 1997.
"I need to make hundreds of phone calls to various ministries just to find out who is responsible for what," Kosmopoulos said.
"I travel to Athens to talk to them face to face about our problems and their standard answer is: Don't worry, by next month there will be progress. This has been going on for years," he added.
